subject: Medicine
summary: Respiratory failure is the inability of the lungs to maintain adequate oxygenation or CO₂ elimination. It is classified by gas abnormalities and severity, and requires rapid identification of cause and supportive care.

sections.p: Respiratory failure occurs when PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (hypoxemic) or PaCO₂ > 50 mmHg with pH < 7.35 (hypercapnic) despite maximal effort. Diagnosis uses arterial blood gas (ABG) and clinical assessment of work of breathing.
b: ABG provides the primary objective criteria.
Look for tachypnea, accessory‑muscle use, altered mental status.

sections.p: The American Thoracic Society grades failure as mild, moderate, or severe based on PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio and PaCO₂ levels. This guides urgency of ventilatory support.
b: Mild: PaO₂ 60‑80 mmHg, PaCO₂ ≤45 mmHg.
Moderate: PaO₂ 40‑60 mmHg or PaCO₂ 45‑60 mmHg.
Severe: PaO₂ <40 mmHg or PaCO₂ >60 mmHg with acidosis.

sections.p: Identify whether the primary problem is hypoxemic (type 1) or hypercapnic (type 2) and then consider common etiologies, especially those seen in low‑resource settings.
b: Type 1: pneumonia, TB, pulmonary embolism, ARDS, severe malaria.
Type 2: COPD exacerbation, asthma status, neuromuscular weakness (GBS, myasthenia), chest wall trauma.
Mixed: sepsis with multi‑organ failure, severe anemia, high‑altitude exposure.

sections.p: Patients develop dyspnea, tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, altered consciousness, and may have a paradoxical rise in PaCO₂ indicating fatigue.
b: Acute: rapid onset, often after infection or asthma attack.
Chronic: progressive dyspnea, weight loss, nocturnal hypoventilation.

sections.p: Targeted tests answer specific questions about gas exchange, underlying disease, and severity.

t.b: What are the oxygenation and ventilation status? Shows PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH; guides need for ventilation.
What structural lung pathology is present? Detects pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, infiltrates.
Is oxygen saturation adequate? Quick bedside screen; if unavailable, use clinical signs.
Is there obstructive airflow limitation? Helps differentiate COPD/asthma from neuromuscular causes.
Is infection or hemolysis contributing? Guides antimicrobial therapy in endemic areas.

sections.p: Recognize signs that herald rapid deterioration and life‑threatening sequelae.
b: Rising PaCO₂ or falling pH despite increased effort.
Severe hypoxemia (SpO₂ < 85%) or hemodynamic instability.
Altered mental status, bradycardia, or impending cardiac arrest.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide ventilatory support and monitor closely. Choose therapies based on pathophysiology and resource availability.
b: Oxygen therapy: titrate to SpO₂ 92‑96% (88‑92% in COPD).
Non‑invasive ventilation (BiPAP) for hypercapnic failure if conscious.
Intubation and mechanical ventilation for severe hypoxemia or exhaustion.
Bronchodilators and steroids for asthma/ COPD exacerbations.
Antibiotics for bacterial pneumonia, anti‑TB drugs for TB, antimalarials for malaria.
Sodium bicarbonate only if metabolic acidosis coexists; not for pure respiratory acidosis.

sections.p: After acute stabilization, address chronic risk factors and arrange monitoring to avoid recurrence.
b: Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal).
Smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation.
Long‑term oxygen for chronic hypoxemia.
Regular review of ventilatory settings and adherence to therapy.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic respiratory failure but have different primary mechanisms.
b: Cardiac failure – presents with dyspnea but primary problem is fluid overload.
Anemia – low oxygen content without gas exchange abnormality.
Severe sepsis – may cause hypoxia but primary driver is circulatory shock.

sections.p: Beware of values that appear normal despite serious pathology.
b: Normal PaCO₂ in a pregnant patient is abnormal (physiologic PaCO₂ is lower).
Pulse oximetry may be falsely high in carbon monoxide poisoning.
ABG may show normal PaO₂ if supplemental O₂ is already given, masking underlying lung disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, or unresponsive patient.
Rapidly rising PaCO₂ (>55 mmHg) or falling pH (<7.30) despite maximal effort.

faq.q: Why does PaCO₂ rise in a patient who looks very breathless?
faq.a: It indicates respiratory muscle fatigue; the patient can no longer increase ventilation.

faq.q: When is non‑invasive ventilation preferred over intubation?
faq.a: When the patient is alert, can protect the airway, and has hypercapnic failure without severe hypoxemia.

faq.q: Can a normal chest X‑ray rule out respiratory failure?
faq.a: No; gas exchange abnormalities can exist with a normal radiograph, especially early in COPD or neuromuscular weakness.

exam: Explain how to differentiate type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure using ABG values.
List the first three most likely causes of acute hypercapnic respiratory failure in a low‑resource setting.
Describe the step‑wise management of a patient with status asthmaticus who develops rising PaCO₂.
